C6_ChemistryMatteranditscompositionSim.title: Gases Do Not Have Any Mass or Weight
C6_ChemistryMatteranditscompositionSim.description: Students often believe that air and other gases have no mass because they are invisible and float freely around us. They assume only solids and liquids count as matter with measurable weight.
C6_ChemistryMatteranditscompositionSim.correction: Air and all gases are matter, meaning they possess mass and occupy space. When a balloon is inflated with air, it becomes heavier than a deflated balloon, demonstrating gas mass. The invisible particles of gas still have weight, even though they are spread far apart.

C6_ChemistryMatteranditscompositionSim.title: Fine Powders and Granules Are Liquids
C6_ChemistryMatteranditscompositionSim.description: Students frequently classify granulated substances like salt, sugar, or sand as liquids because they can be poured and take the shape of their container. They confuse the collective behavior of small solids with liquid flow.
C6_ChemistryMatteranditscompositionSim.correction: Granules of salt or sand are small individual solids, each maintaining a fixed shape and definite volume. While a collection of granules flows together, a single grain does not change its shape to match the container. Therefore, powders are classified as solids, not liquids.

C6_ChemistryMatteranditscompositionSim.title: Dissolved Substances Disappear and Stop Existing
C6_ChemistryMatteranditscompositionSim.description: When a solid like sugar or salt dissolves completely in water, students think the solid has disappeared and no longer exists. They believe dissolving is a process where matter is destroyed.
C6_ChemistryMatteranditscompositionSim.correction: Dissolving is a physical change where solid particles break apart and spread evenly between liquid particles without being destroyed. The dissolved substance retains its chemical identity and mass, which can be proven by tasting the solution or evaporating the liquid to recover the solid. Thus, total mass is conserved during dissolution.

C6_ChemistryMatteranditscompositionSim.title: Compounds Retain Properties of Their Constituent Elements
C6_ChemistryMatteranditscompositionSim.description: Students often think that a compound like water retains the individual properties of hydrogen and oxygen, just as a mixture does. They assume chemical combining is identical to physical mixing.
C6_ChemistryMatteranditscompositionSim.correction: In a compound, elements combine chemically in a fixed ratio to form an entirely new substance with unique properties. For example, explosive hydrogen gas and oxygen gas combine to form water, which extinguishes fires. Unlike physical mixtures, constituent elements lose their original properties when forming a compound.

C6_ChemistryMatteranditscompositionSim.title: Changes of State Are Chemical Changes
C6_ChemistryMatteranditscompositionSim.description: Students often assume that changing state from ice to water produces a brand-new chemical substance because the appearance changes dramatically. They view state changes as irreversible chemical reactions.
C6_ChemistryMatteranditscompositionSim.correction: Phase changes like melting, freezing, and boiling are physical changes because no new substance is formed. Ice, liquid water, and steam are all composed of the exact same chemical molecules. Only the energy and distance between the particles change during these reversible processes.

C7_ChemistryAtomicstructureelectronsprot.title: Electrons and Protons Have Equal Mass in Neutral Atoms
C7_ChemistryAtomicstructureelectronsprot.description: Students believe that since an atom is neutral, electrons and protons must have equal mass as well as equal charge. They assume a proton and an electron weigh the same amount.
C7_ChemistryAtomicstructureelectronsprot.correction: While an atom is neutral because a proton's +1 charge balances an electron's -1 charge, their masses are drastically different. A proton is nearly 1840 times heavier than an electron, whose mass is considered negligible in atomic mass calculations. Protons and neutrons together account for almost the entire mass of an atom.

C7_ChemistryAtomicstructureelectronsprot.title: Atomic Number Represents Total Subatomic Particles in an Atom
C7_ChemistryAtomicstructureelectronsprot.description: Students often confuse atomic number with total particle count, believing it includes protons, neutrons, and electrons combined. They mistake the atomic number for the total sum of all particles inside an atom.
C7_ChemistryAtomicstructureelectronsprot.correction: The atomic number of an element is strictly defined as the number of protons present in the nucleus of its atom. In a neutral atom, this also equals the number of electrons, but it never includes neutrons or total particle sums. The total count of protons and neutrons combined is referred to as the mass number.

C7_ChemistryAtomicstructureelectronsprot.title: Isotopes Are Completely Different Chemical Elements from Each Other
C7_ChemistryAtomicstructureelectronsprot.description: Students believe that changing the number of neutrons in an atom transforms it into a completely different chemical element. They assume any change in subatomic particle numbers alters the identity of the element.
C7_ChemistryAtomicstructureelectronsprot.correction: The identity of an element is determined exclusively by its atomic number, which is the number of protons. Isotopes are atoms of the very same element that possess equal numbers of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Because they have identical proton and electron configurations, isotopes exhibit nearly identical chemical properties.

C7_ChemistryAtomicstructureelectronsprot.title: Electron Shells Can Accommodate Any Number of Electrons Randomly
C7_ChemistryAtomicstructureelectronsprot.description: Students assume electrons are randomly distributed in the atom or that any shell can hold an unlimited number of electrons. They often believe all shells have identical electron capacities.
C7_ChemistryAtomicstructureelectronsprot.correction: Electrons fill specific energy levels or shells according to defined rules, such as the 2n² formula where n is the shell number. The first shell (K shell) can hold a maximum of 2 electrons, while the second shell (L shell) can hold up to 8 electrons. Electrons systematically occupy lower energy inner shells completely before entering outer shells.

C7_ChemistryAtomicstructureelectronsprot.title: Neutrons Carry an Electric Charge to Help Balance Atoms
C7_ChemistryAtomicstructureelectronsprot.description: Students frequently assume neutrons must carry a weak positive or negative charge to help balance the atom electrically. They struggle to comprehend a subatomic particle existing with zero charge.
C7_ChemistryAtomicstructureelectronsprot.correction: Neutrons are neutral subatomic particles that carry no electric charge at all. Electrical neutrality in an atom is achieved solely by having an equal number of positively charged protons and negatively charged electrons. Neutrons reside in the nucleus to add stability by reducing electrostatic repulsion between positively charged protons.

C6_ChemistryCarbondioxideandnitrogeninai.title: Humans breathe only oxygen and exhale only carbon dioxide
C6_ChemistryCarbondioxideandnitrogeninai.description: Students often believe that inhaled air consists strictly of pure oxygen and exhaled air contains strictly carbon dioxide. They assume nitrogen and other gases are filtered out before entering the lungs.
C6_ChemistryCarbondioxideandnitrogeninai.correction: Inhaled air is the normal atmospheric mixture containing 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and tiny amounts of other gases. The body absorbs only a portion of the oxygen and releases carbon dioxide into the exhaled mixture. Therefore, exhaled air still contains mostly nitrogen along with about 16% oxygen and 4% carbon dioxide.

C6_ChemistryCarbondioxideandnitrogeninai.title: Plants absorb nitrogen gas directly from air through their leaves
C6_ChemistryCarbondioxideandnitrogeninai.description: Since nitrogen makes up 78% of the air, students assume plants absorb it directly through leaf stomata just as they do with carbon dioxide.
C6_ChemistryCarbondioxideandnitrogeninai.correction: Plants cannot use elemental nitrogen gas directly from the atmosphere. They rely on nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the soil or root nodules to convert atmospheric nitrogen into usable nitrogen compounds like nitrates. Plants then absorb these dissolved compounds through their root system to synthesize proteins.

C6_ChemistryCarbondioxideandnitrogeninai.title: Plants use carbon dioxide for respiration instead of oxygen gas
C6_ChemistryCarbondioxideandnitrogeninai.description: Students confuse photosynthesis with respiration and believe plants breathe in carbon dioxide and breathe out oxygen continuously without needing oxygen.
C6_ChemistryCarbondioxideandnitrogeninai.correction: Plants perform photosynthesis to prepare food using carbon dioxide, but like all living organisms, they also perform respiration day and night using oxygen to release energy. During daytime, the oxygen produced by photosynthesis exceeds the oxygen consumed by respiration, which conceals the fact that plants are using oxygen.

C6_ChemistryCarbondioxideandnitrogeninai.title: The greenhouse effect is entirely harmful to Earth's survival
C6_ChemistryCarbondioxideandnitrogeninai.description: Students frequently view the greenhouse effect solely as a dangerous environmental problem caused by human pollution that must be completely eliminated.
C6_ChemistryCarbondioxideandnitrogeninai.correction: The natural greenhouse effect is an essential process that traps heat to keep Earth warm enough to sustain life. Without naturally occurring greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide, Earth's average temperature would drop to around -18°C. Environmental harm occurs only when excessive human activities increase carbon dioxide levels, causing global warming beyond normal limits.

C6_ChemistryCarbondioxideandnitrogeninai.title: Carbon dioxide makes up a large percentage of atmospheric air
C6_ChemistryCarbondioxideandnitrogeninai.description: Because carbon dioxide is heavily emphasized in lessons about photosynthesis and climate change, students often assume it forms a major fraction of the air.
C6_ChemistryCarbondioxideandnitrogeninai.correction: Carbon dioxide is a trace gas that makes up only about 0.04% of Earth's atmosphere by volume. Nitrogen (78%) and oxygen (21%) together make up almost 99% of the total air. Despite its very small percentage, carbon dioxide plays a critical role in sustaining plant life and maintaining global thermal balance.

C6_ChemistryAtomicstructuresubatomicpart.title: Atoms Are Solid Spheres with No Internal Parts
C6_ChemistryAtomicstructuresubatomicpart.description: Students often believe that atoms are hard, indivisible, solid spheres similar to marbles or billiard balls. They think atoms have no internal components or subatomic particles inside them.
C6_ChemistryAtomicstructuresubatomicpart.correction: Dalton originally proposed that atoms were indivisible spheres, but later discoveries proved this concept incomplete. An atom actually consists of a central nucleus surrounded by tiny electrons moving around it. The nucleus itself is made up of smaller subatomic particles called protons and neutrons.

C6_ChemistryAtomicstructuresubatomicpart.title: Atoms Are Completely Filled with No Empty Space
C6_ChemistryAtomicstructuresubatomicpart.description: Students frequently assume that an atom is packed tightly with subatomic particles, leaving no open space inside. They imagine the inside of an atom as a dense, fully packed solid sphere.
C6_ChemistryAtomicstructuresubatomicpart.correction: In reality, an atom is composed almost entirely of empty space. The tiny nucleus occupies a minuscule volume at the center, while electrons move at relatively large distances around it. If the nucleus were the size of a marble, the entire atom would be larger than a football stadium.

C6_ChemistryAtomicstructuresubatomicpart.title: Protons Neutrons and Electrons Have Equal Mass
C6_ChemistryAtomicstructuresubatomicpart.description: Students often think all subatomic particles are equal in size and mass because they are all tiny components of an atom. They assume an electron weighs the same as a proton or neutron.
C6_ChemistryAtomicstructuresubatomicpart.correction: Protons and neutrons have nearly equal mass and account for almost all of an atom's weight. In contrast, an electron is extremely light, having roughly 1/1836th the mass of a proton. Because of this, the mass of electrons is considered negligible when calculating atomic mass.

C6_ChemistryAtomicstructuresubatomicpart.title: Dalton Theory Proves Atoms Can Never Be Divided
C6_ChemistryAtomicstructuresubatomicpart.description: Students often believe that John Dalton's original statement about atoms being ultimate indivisible units remains completely true today. They think it is physically impossible for an atom to be broken down.
C6_ChemistryAtomicstructuresubatomicpart.correction: Dalton's atomic theory was a major breakthrough, but modern chemistry has modified his postulate on indivisibility. Scientists discovered that atoms can be divided into subatomic particles such as protons, neutrons, and electrons. Furthermore, nuclear reactions are capable of splitting atomic nuclei into smaller fragments.

C6_ChemistryAtomicstructuresubatomicpart.title: Electrons Orbit Nucleus Exactly Like Planets Around Sun
C6_ChemistryAtomicstructuresubatomicpart.description: Students frequently picture electrons moving along fixed, rigid circular tracks around the nucleus, just like planets orbiting the Sun. They assume electrons follow strict, predictable 2D paths.
C6_ChemistryAtomicstructuresubatomicpart.correction: While the solar system analogy helps introduce atomic structure, electrons do not move along fixed two-dimensional tracks. Instead, electrons move extremely fast in three-dimensional regions called shells or energy levels around the nucleus. Modern atomic models describe these movements as clouds of electron probability rather than simple circular orbits.

C8_ChemistryMatterstatesandinterconversi.title: Believing Evaporation Occurs Only at the Boiling Point
C8_ChemistryMatterstatesandinterconversi.description: Students often confuse evaporation with boiling and believe that liquids turn into gas only when heated to their boiling point. They fail to recognize that evaporation happens continuously at any temperature.
C8_ChemistryMatterstatesandinterconversi.correction: Evaporation is a surface phenomenon that occurs at all temperatures below the boiling point, where surface particles with higher kinetic energy escape into the air. Boiling, in contrast, is a bulk phenomenon that occurs only at a specific temperature throughout the entire liquid body.

C8_ChemistryMatterstatesandinterconversi.title: Assuming Temperature Rises Continuously During Phase Transitions
C8_ChemistryMatterstatesandinterconversi.description: Students commonly believe that while ice is actively melting or water is boiling, the temperature keeps rising as long as heat is supplied. They assume heat addition always results in a temperature increase.
C8_ChemistryMatterstatesandinterconversi.correction: During a state change, the temperature remains completely constant despite continuous heating. The absorbed heat energy, known as latent heat, is used solely to break the intermolecular forces of attraction rather than raising particle kinetic energy.

C8_ChemistryMatterstatesandinterconversi.title: Thinking Water Droplets Outside Cold Glass Leak from Inside
C8_ChemistryMatterstatesandinterconversi.description: Students frequently think that the water droplets appearing on the outer surface of a cold drink glass have seeped or leaked through the solid walls from the inside. They misinterpret the origin of the condensed liquid.
C8_ChemistryMatterstatesandinterconversi.correction: The water droplets originate from invisible water vapor present in the surrounding atmospheric air. When these gaseous water molecules touch the cold outer surface of the glass, they lose kinetic energy and undergo condensation to form liquid droplets.

C8_ChemistryMatterstatesandinterconversi.title: Believing Sublimation Involves an Unseen Microscopic Liquid Phase
C8_ChemistryMatterstatesandinterconversi.description: Students often assume that sublimating substances, such as camphor or dry ice, actually melt into a very brief or invisible liquid phase before rapidly turning into gas. They struggle to accept that the liquid phase is skipped entirely.
C8_ChemistryMatterstatesandinterconversi.correction: Sublimation is the direct conversion of a solid into a gas without passing through an intermediate liquid state. In sublimating solids, the intermolecular forces are weak enough that heating provides sufficient energy to completely separate the particles directly into the gaseous state.

C8_ChemistryMatterstatesandinterconversi.title: Mistaking Individual Particle Expansion for Volume Expansion Upon Heating
C8_ChemistryMatterstatesandinterconversi.description: Students often believe that when matter is heated during phase changes, the individual atoms or molecules expand in size. They think solid particles physically swell to become larger liquid or gas particles.
C8_ChemistryMatterstatesandinterconversi.correction: The individual particles themselves do not grow or change in size when heated. Instead, heating increases the kinetic energy of the particles, causing them to move faster and push farther apart, which increases the intermolecular space and overall volume.

C7_ChemistryMatterclassificationrevisite.title: Thinking any substance made of molecules must be a compound
C7_ChemistryMatterclassificationrevisite.description: Students often believe that if a substance exists as molecules, such as oxygen gas or ozone, it must be a compound. They assume elements can only exist as single, unbonded individual atoms.
C7_ChemistryMatterclassificationrevisite.correction: An element consists of only one type of atom, but these identical atoms can join together to form molecules like O2 or N2. A compound, by contrast, requires two or more different types of elements chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio. Therefore, molecules can represent both elements and compounds depending on atom variety.

C7_ChemistryMatterclassificationrevisite.title: Believing compounds retain properties of their constituent elements
C7_ChemistryMatterclassificationrevisite.description: Students frequently think that a compound exhibits a combination of the physical and chemical properties of its individual elements. For example, they expect water (H2O) to support burning because it contains oxygen gas.
C7_ChemistryMatterclassificationrevisite.correction: When elements chemically combine to form a compound, a chemical change occurs that forms a completely new substance with unique properties. The original properties of the constituent elements are entirely lost during this reaction. In contrast, only physical mixtures retain the individual properties of their constituent parts.

C7_ChemistryMatterclassificationrevisite.title: Classifying colloids like milk as homogeneous true solutions
C7_ChemistryMatterclassificationrevisite.description: Students often assume that because liquids like milk, ink, or fog look uniform to the naked eye, they are true homogeneous solutions. They confuse visual smoothness with uniform distribution at the particle level.
C7_ChemistryMatterclassificationrevisite.correction: Colloids appear uniform to the naked eye, but they are actually heterogeneous mixtures containing tiny dispersed particles that do not settle. These particles are larger than those in a true solution and scatter light, creating the Tyndall effect. Under high magnification, the distinct phases of a colloid become clearly visible.

C7_ChemistryMatterclassificationrevisite.title: Assuming dissolved solids in solutions disappear or form compounds
C7_ChemistryMatterclassificationrevisite.description: Many students believe that when salt or sugar dissolves completely in water, the solid is permanently destroyed or turned into liquid. Others confuse dissolution with a chemical reaction that creates a brand-new compound.
C7_ChemistryMatterclassificationrevisite.correction: Dissolving is a physical process where solute particles separate and fit into spaces between solvent particles without changing chemically. The solid solute is still present throughout the liquid mixture and retains its identity. This is proven because the original solid can be recovered unchanged using simple physical evaporation.

C7_ChemistryMatterclassificationrevisite.title: Believing compounds can be separated using physical separation methods
C7_ChemistryMatterclassificationrevisite.description: Students often confuse compounds with mixtures and think that elements in a compound can be separated using physical techniques like filtration or evaporation.
C7_ChemistryMatterclassificationrevisite.correction: The elements in a compound are joined together by strong chemical bonds that cannot be broken by physical separation methods. Only chemical reactions or electrochemical processes, such as electrolysis, can decompose a compound into its constituent elements. Physical methods like filtration can only separate the components of physical mixtures.

C7_ChemistryWaterauniversalsolventSim.title: Water as a universal solvent can dissolve absolutely every substance
C7_ChemistryWaterauniversalsolventSim.description: Students believe that because water is called a 'universal solvent', it can dissolve every liquid, solid, and gas, including oil, wax, and sand.
C7_ChemistryWaterauniversalsolventSim.correction: Water is termed a universal solvent because it dissolves more substances than any other liquid, but it cannot dissolve everything. Substances like oil, petrol, and sand are insoluble in water due to differences in their chemical nature.

C7_ChemistryWaterauniversalsolventSim.title: Hard water is physically hard to touch or contains ice
C7_ChemistryWaterauniversalsolventSim.description: Students often confuse the term 'hard water' with ice or assume it feels physically rigid, rough, or solid against the skin.
C7_ChemistryWaterauniversalsolventSim.correction: Hard water refers to liquid water that contains high concentrations of dissolved minerals, primarily calcium and magnesium salts. It looks and feels like ordinary water, but it does not readily form lather when mixed with soap.

C7_ChemistryWaterauniversalsolventSim.title: Dissolving a solid in water is identical to melting it
C7_ChemistryWaterauniversalsolventSim.description: Students frequently think that when sugar or salt disappears in water, it has melted because of the liquid environment.
C7_ChemistryWaterauniversalsolventSim.correction: Melting is a phase change caused by heat converting a single solid into liquid form. Dissolving happens when solvent molecules interact with solute particles, breaking them apart and distributing them evenly throughout the liquid.

C7_ChemistryWaterauniversalsolventSim.title: Clear and transparent water is always pure and safe drinking water
C7_ChemistryWaterauniversalsolventSim.description: Students often assume that if water looks completely clear and free of mud or dirt, it is completely pure and safe to consume.
C7_ChemistryWaterauniversalsolventSim.correction: Water can appear perfectly clear while still containing invisible dissolved chemical pollutants, toxic heavy metals, or harmful pathogens. True purity requires specialized filtration and purification methods beyond simple visual inspection.

C7_ChemistryWaterauniversalsolventSim.title: Boiling polluted water removes all types of harmful contaminants
C7_ChemistryWaterauniversalsolventSim.description: Students believe that boiling water purifies it completely by eliminating both biological pathogens and chemical pollutants.
C7_ChemistryWaterauniversalsolventSim.correction: Boiling effectively kills micro-organisms such as bacteria and viruses present in water. However, it cannot remove dissolved chemical pollutants, pesticides, or heavy metals, which actually become more concentrated as steam evaporates.

C8_ChemistryChemicalequationsbalancingSi.title: Changing Subscripts in Formulas to Balance Chemical Equations
C8_ChemistryChemicalequationsbalancingSi.description: Students often alter the subscript numbers inside a chemical formula to balance atoms on both sides of an equation. They believe subscript numbers can be freely adjusted just like coefficients.
C8_ChemistryChemicalequationsbalancingSi.correction: Subscripts define the fixed chemical identity and composition of a specific compound, so changing them alters the substance entirely. To balance a chemical equation correctly, students must only place whole-number coefficients in front of the chemical formulas. This ensures atom counts are equalized without changing the actual chemical species involved.

C8_ChemistryChemicalequationsbalancingSi.title: Mass Is Lost When Reactions Produce Gas Products
C8_ChemistryChemicalequationsbalancingSi.description: Students frequently believe that the Law of Conservation of Mass is violated when a reaction produces a gas and the remaining mixture weighs less. They assume that mass disappears during gaseous reactions.
C8_ChemistryChemicalequationsbalancingSi.correction: According to the Law of Conservation of Mass, matter can neither be created nor destroyed during a chemical reaction. When gas escapes into the surroundings from an open container, its mass is simply lost to the air, not destroyed. If the reaction is carried out in a sealed vessel, the total mass of reactants and products remains identical.

C8_ChemistryChemicalequationsbalancingSi.title: Coefficients Apply Only to the Immediately Adjacent Element
C8_ChemistryChemicalequationsbalancingSi.description: Students often assume a coefficient placed in front of a chemical formula multiplies only the first atom or symbol. For example, they interpret 2H2O as having four hydrogens but only one oxygen atom.
C8_ChemistryChemicalequationsbalancingSi.correction: A coefficient written before a formula acts as a multiplier for every atom present in that entire molecule or formula unit. For example, 2H2O represents two complete water molecules, containing a total of four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms. Understanding this distributive property is essential for accurately counting atoms during equation balancing.

C8_ChemistryChemicalequationsbalancingSi.title: Equal Number of Molecules Required on Both Sides
C8_ChemistryChemicalequationsbalancingSi.description: Students often confuse the conservation of atoms with a conservation of total molecules, expecting equal molecule counts on reactant and product sides. They believe an equation with two reactant molecules must yield exactly two product molecules.
C8_ChemistryChemicalequationsbalancingSi.correction: The Law of Conservation of Mass dictates that the total number of each type of atom must remain equal before and after a reaction. Molecules, however, break apart and rearrange into entirely new combinations, meaning the total number of molecules can change. Balancing focuses strictly on conserving individual atoms, not the total molecule count.

C8_ChemistryChemicalequationsbalancingSi.title: The Reaction Arrow Functions as a Mathematical Equals Sign
C8_ChemistryChemicalequationsbalancingSi.description: Students frequently view the reaction arrow (→) as a standard mathematical equals sign (=) indicating simple numeric equality. They assume reactants and products are interchangeable substances on either side.
C8_ChemistryChemicalequationsbalancingSi.correction: The reaction arrow in a chemical equation represents a directional transformation from starting materials (reactants) into new substances (products). It indicates the pathway and direction in which a chemical change proceeds, rather than a reversible mathematical equivalence. Using an equals sign obscures the fundamental concept that reactants undergo a chemical conversion.

C9_ChemistryEnergychangesinchemicalreact.title: Chemical bond breaking releases energy to the surroundings
C9_ChemistryEnergychangesinchemicalreact.description: Students often believe that breaking a chemical bond releases energy, confusing chemical bonds with physical objects like stretched rubber bands that snap and release energy.
C9_ChemistryEnergychangesinchemicalreact.correction: Breaking chemical bonds always requires an input of energy to overcome the attractive forces between atoms. Conversely, energy is only released when new chemical bonds are formed. The overall energy change of a reaction depends on whether bond breaking absorbs more energy than bond formation releases.

C9_ChemistryEnergychangesinchemicalreact.title: Only endothermic reactions need activation energy to start
C9_ChemistryEnergychangesinchemicalreact.description: Many students think that only endothermic reactions require an initial energy input, while exothermic reactions start spontaneously without any energy input.
C9_ChemistryEnergychangesinchemicalreact.correction: All chemical reactions, whether exothermic or endothermic, require activation energy to break existing reactant bonds and begin. For example, wood burning is highly exothermic, but it still requires a match flame to provide the initial activation energy to start the reaction. Once started, exothermic reactions generate enough heat to provide activation energy for remaining reactants.

C9_ChemistryEnergychangesinchemicalreact.title: Energy is created or lost during chemical energy changes
C9_ChemistryEnergychangesinchemicalreact.description: Students often assume that the heat produced in exothermic reactions is newly created energy rather than transformed chemical energy.
C9_ChemistryEnergychangesinchemicalreact.correction: According to the Law of Conservation of Energy, energy cannot be created or destroyed during chemical reactions. In exothermic reactions, stored chemical potential energy in reactant bonds is converted into thermal energy. In endothermic reactions, thermal energy absorbed from surroundings is transformed into chemical potential energy in product bonds.

C9_ChemistryEnergychangesinchemicalreact.title: All chemical reactions result in a rise in temperature
C9_ChemistryEnergychangesinchemicalreact.description: Students frequently believe that any chemical reaction will cause the reaction vessel or surrounding solution to feel warm.
C9_ChemistryEnergychangesinchemicalreact.correction: Chemical reactions can cause temperatures to either rise or fall depending on the net energy change. Endothermic reactions absorb heat from their surroundings, causing the temperature of the reaction mixture to drop noticeably. A common example is dissolving ammonium chloride in water, which cools the solution down.

C9_ChemistryEnergychangesinchemicalreact.title: Activation energy determines the net overall chemical enthalpy change
C9_ChemistryEnergychangesinchemicalreact.description: Students often confuse activation energy with enthalpy change, believing that a high activation energy means the reaction must be endothermic overall.
C9_ChemistryEnergychangesinchemicalreact.correction: Enthalpy change is the net difference between the energy of the reactants and the energy of the products. Activation energy is merely the initial energy barrier that must be overcome to reach the transition state. A reaction can have a very high activation energy and still be strongly exothermic overall once it proceeds.

C8_ChemistryWaterpropertiesandcompositio.title: Ice is denser than liquid water because it is solid
C8_ChemistryWaterpropertiesandcompositio.description: Students believe that since ice is a solid, it must be denser than liquid water and sink. They assume that all substances in their solid state are denser than their liquid state.
C8_ChemistryWaterpropertiesandcompositio.correction: Water exhibits anomalous expansion, expanding when it freezes into ice due to the formation of an open cage-like crystal structure. This makes ice less dense than liquid water, allowing it to float. Consequently, liquid water reaches its maximum density at 4°C, not at its freezing point.

C8_ChemistryWaterpropertiesandcompositio.title: Boiling water breaks chemical bonds to form hydrogen and oxygen
C8_ChemistryWaterpropertiesandcompositio.description: Students often confuse phase changes with chemical reactions, believing that boiling breaks the H₂O molecule into hydrogen and oxygen gases. They think steam is a mixture of separate hydrogen and oxygen atoms.
C8_ChemistryWaterpropertiesandcompositio.correction: Boiling is a physical change that breaks weak intermolecular forces between water molecules, not the strong covalent bonds within them. Steam consists of gaseous H₂O molecules that retain the exact chemical composition of liquid water. Chemical decomposition of water into hydrogen and oxygen requires electrolysis, not simple heating.

C8_ChemistryWaterpropertiesandcompositio.title: Electrolysis yields equal volumes of hydrogen and oxygen gas
C8_ChemistryWaterpropertiesandcompositio.description: Students assume that electrolysis produces equal volumes of hydrogen and oxygen gas because water is made of two elements. They overlook the atomic ratio represented in the chemical formula.
C8_ChemistryWaterpropertiesandcompositio.correction: The chemical formula of water is H₂O, meaning it contains two hydrogen atoms for every one oxygen atom. During electrolysis, hydrogen gas collects at the cathode and oxygen gas at the anode in a 2:1 volume ratio. Therefore, the volume of hydrogen gas produced is double the volume of oxygen gas.

C8_ChemistryWaterpropertiesandcompositio.title: Water should burn because it contains hydrogen and oxygen
C8_ChemistryWaterpropertiesandcompositio.description: Students believe water must be combustible because hydrogen is highly flammable and oxygen supports burning. They expect a chemical compound to retain the properties of its constituent elements.
C8_ChemistryWaterpropertiesandcompositio.correction: When hydrogen and oxygen chemically combine to form water, a compound with entirely new properties is produced. Water is actually the stable product of hydrogen combustion, meaning it cannot burn further under normal conditions. As a result, water acts as a fire extinguisher rather than a fuel.

C8_ChemistryWaterpropertiesandcompositio.title: Water always boils at 100 degrees Celsius everywhere
C8_ChemistryWaterpropertiesandcompositio.description: Students think 100°C is an absolute, unchangeable boiling point for water in all situations. They fail to realize how atmospheric pressure and dissolved impurities alter boiling behavior.
C8_ChemistryWaterpropertiesandcompositio.correction: The boiling point of pure water is 100°C only at standard atmospheric pressure (1 atm). At higher altitudes where atmospheric pressure is lower, water boils at temperatures below 100°C. Additionally, adding dissolved solutes like common salt increases the boiling point of water above 100°C.

C9_ChemistryAcidraincompositionandcauses.title: Pure Rain is Completely Neutral with a pH of 7.0
C9_ChemistryAcidraincompositionandcauses.description: Students often believe that unpolluted rain is strictly neutral with a pH of 7.0, and any degree of acidity makes it acid rain.
C9_ChemistryAcidraincompositionandcauses.correction: Normal rainwater is naturally slightly acidic with a pH of around 5.6 due to dissolved atmospheric carbon dioxide forming weak carbonic acid. Rain is technically classified as acid rain only when its pH falls below 5.6 due to atmospheric reactions involving sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides. Therefore, a slight natural acidity is standard, but strong mineral acids cause true acid rain.

C9_ChemistryAcidraincompositionandcauses.title: Acid Rain Causes Severe Instant Chemical Burns on Human Skin
C9_ChemistryAcidraincompositionandcauses.description: Students frequently imagine that acid rain acts like concentrated laboratory acid, immediately burning human skin or clothes upon direct contact.
C9_ChemistryAcidraincompositionandcauses.correction: Acid rain is far too dilute to burn human skin or cause immediate physical pain upon contact. The primary danger of acid rain lies in its gradual, long-term ecological destruction, such as leaching soil nutrients, harming aquatic ecosystems, and eroding marble structures over time. Walking in acid rain carries no greater direct chemical burn risk to skin than walking in normal rain.

C9_ChemistryAcidraincompositionandcauses.title: Carbon Dioxide Emission is the Main Cause of Acid Rain
C9_ChemistryAcidraincompositionandcauses.description: Students often confuse greenhouse gases with acid-forming pollutants and assume carbon dioxide is the primary cause of acid rain.
C9_ChemistryAcidraincompositionandcauses.correction: Carbon dioxide forms weak carbonic acid, which accounts only for the natural, baseline acidity of unpolluted rain. True acid rain is primarily caused by industrial emissions of sulfur dioxide (SO2) and nitrogen oxides (NOx) produced from burning fossil fuels in power plants and vehicles. In the atmosphere, these gases react with oxygen and water to form much stronger acids, namely sulfuric acid (H2SO4) and nitric acid (HNO3).

C9_ChemistryAcidraincompositionandcauses.title: Acid Rain Only Falls Directly Over Industrial and Urban Areas
C9_ChemistryAcidraincompositionandcauses.description: Students assume that acid rain occurs exclusively in the immediate geographical locations where factories and vehicles emit pollutants.
C9_ChemistryAcidraincompositionandcauses.correction: Atmospheric wind currents can transport precursor gases like sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides hundreds of kilometers away from their original industrial sources before precipitation occurs. Consequently, pristine rural environments, mountain lakes, and remote forests far from urban centers frequently suffer severe damage from acid rain. The environmental impact is widespread and not limited to the site of industrial emissions.

C9_ChemistryAcidraincompositionandcauses.title: Acid Rain Consists Entirely of Pure Undiluted Strong Acids
C9_ChemistryAcidraincompositionandcauses.description: Students sometimes believe that clouds store pure sulfuric or nitric acid that falls down as liquid acid rather than rain.
C9_ChemistryAcidraincompositionandcauses.correction: Acid rain is standard water precipitation that contains very low concentrations of dissolved mineral acids. While these trace acids lower the rainwater's pH to values typically between 4.0 and 5.0, the precipitation remains overwhelmingly composed of water molecules. The term describes rain with increased hydrogen ion concentration, not concentrated atmospheric acid.

C9_ChemistryCovalentbondingSim.title: Covalent bonds involve full transfer of electrons between atoms
C9_ChemistryCovalentbondingSim.description: Students often confuse covalent bonding with ionic bonding, believing that one atom completely gives away its valence electrons to another. They assume electron sharing is identical to permanent electron transfer.
C9_ChemistryCovalentbondingSim.correction: In covalent bonding, non-metal atoms share one or more pairs of valence electrons to achieve a stable octet without transferring electrons. Both participating nuclei exert an electrostatic attraction on the shared electron pairs to remain bonded. This mutual sharing allows both atoms to simultaneously fill their outermost electron shells.

C9_ChemistryCovalentbondingSim.title: Double covalent bonds are twice as strong as single bonds
C9_ChemistryCovalentbondingSim.description: Students frequently assume that a double bond consists of two identical single bonds, making it exactly twice as strong. Consequently, they believe bond strength increases in exact linear multiples as bond order increases.
C9_ChemistryCovalentbondingSim.correction: A double covalent bond consists of one strong sigma bond and one weaker pi bond, which are formed by different types of atomic orbital overlap. Because a pi bond is intrinsically weaker than a sigma bond, a double bond is stronger than a single bond but not twice as strong. Therefore, bond dissociation energy does not scale in simple integer multiples.

C9_ChemistryCovalentbondingSim.title: Shared electrons in Lewis structures belong to one atom entirely
C9_ChemistryCovalentbondingSim.description: When drawing Lewis dot structures, students often think that shared electron pairs belong exclusively to the more electronegative atom. They view the shared dots as being fully gained by one atom and lost by the other.
C9_ChemistryCovalentbondingSim.correction: Lewis structures use dot pairs or lines between chemical symbols to represent valence electrons shared mutually between bonded atoms. Even when electron density is shifted unequally in a polar bond, the electrons spend time around both nuclei and count toward both octets. Formal or partial charges indicate shifting electron density, not a complete loss of ownership.

C9_ChemistryCovalentbondingSim.title: Polar covalent molecules contain full positive and negative ionic charges
C9_ChemistryCovalentbondingSim.description: Students commonly confuse partial charges in polar covalent molecules with full ionic charges. They believe that polar covalent compounds contain discrete positive and negative ions just like ionic salts do.
C9_ChemistryCovalentbondingSim.correction: Polarity arises when shared electrons are pulled closer to the more electronegative atom, creating an asymmetric distribution of electron density. This unequal sharing results only in small partial charges (delta positive and delta negative), not complete integer charges. The molecule as a whole remains electrically neutral and does not dissociate into separate ions.

C9_ChemistryCovalentbondingSim.title: Covalent bonds break when simple covalent compounds melt or boil
C9_ChemistryCovalentbondingSim.description: Students frequently believe that heating a simple covalent substance breaks the strong covalent bonds holding its constituent atoms together. For example, they think boiling liquid water chemically decomposes H2O molecules into hydrogen and oxygen gases.
C9_ChemistryCovalentbondingSim.correction: Phase changes in simple covalent substances only overcome weak intermolecular forces operating between adjacent molecules. The strong intramolecular covalent bonds holding the individual atoms together within each molecule remain completely intact. Consequently, boiling liquid water produces gaseous steam composed of identical H2O molecules.

C9_ChemistrySoftwaterandhardwaterSim.title: Boiling Removes All Types of Water Hardness Completely
C9_ChemistrySoftwaterandhardwaterSim.description: Students often believe that simply boiling water converts both temporary and permanent hard water into soft water. They view boiling as a universal solution for removing all dissolved salts from hard water.
C9_ChemistrySoftwaterandhardwaterSim.correction: Boiling only removes temporary hardness by decomposing soluble calcium and magnesium hydrogen carbonates into insoluble carbonates. Permanent hardness, caused by chlorides and sulfates of calcium and magnesium, remains unchanged upon boiling. Removing permanent hardness requires chemical treatment, such as adding washing soda or using ion-exchange resins.

C9_ChemistrySoftwaterandhardwaterSim.title: Scum is Dirt Removed From Clothes by Soap
C9_ChemistrySoftwaterandhardwaterSim.description: Students frequently confuse the insoluble white curdy precipitate (scum) formed in hard water with dirt being washed off clothes. They assume that a higher amount of scum indicates more effective cleaning by the soap.
C9_ChemistrySoftwaterandhardwaterSim.correction: Scum is not dirt; it is an insoluble substance formed when soap reacts with calcium and magnesium ions in hard water. This reaction wastes soap and prevents it from forming lather until all hardness ions are precipitated. Synthetic detergents avoid this issue because their calcium and magnesium salts are soluble in water.

C9_ChemistrySoftwaterandhardwaterSim.title: Boiler Scale Helps Insulate and Protect Water Pipes
C9_ChemistrySoftwaterandhardwaterSim.description: Students sometimes think that the thick mineral deposit (scale) inside heating kettles and industrial boilers forms a protective shield that strengthens the metal walls.
C9_ChemistrySoftwaterandhardwaterSim.correction: Boiler scale is composed of insoluble precipitates like calcium carbonate deposited when hard water is heated. Because scale is an extremely poor conductor of heat, it leads to severe energy loss and inefficient heating. Furthermore, localized overheating beneath the scale layer can cause metal boilers to crack or explode under high pressure.

C9_ChemistrySoftwaterandhardwaterSim.title: Ion Exchange Resins Filter Hardness Ions Out Mechanically
C9_ChemistrySoftwaterandhardwaterSim.description: Students often imagine that an ion-exchange resin column softens water by physically trapping hardness-causing minerals like a fine sieve or mesh filter.
C9_ChemistrySoftwaterandhardwaterSim.correction: Ion exchange is a chemical displacement process rather than physical filtration. Calcium and magnesium ions in the hard water chemically replace sodium or hydrogen ions present on the surface of the resin matrix. Once the resin becomes saturated with hardness ions, it must be regenerated using a concentrated sodium chloride solution.

C9_ChemistrySoftwaterandhardwaterSim.title: Soft Water Is Pure Water Free of All Minerals
C9_ChemistrySoftwaterandhardwaterSim.description: Students commonly equate soft water with distilled or pure water, believing that soft water contains no dissolved salts or chemical ions whatsoever.
C9_ChemistrySoftwaterandhardwaterSim.correction: Soft water is defined strictly by its ability to readily form lather with soap due to the absence of calcium and magnesium ions. It may still contain significant quantities of other soluble salts, such as sodium chloride or sodium bicarbonate. Therefore, softened water is chemically distinct from pure or distilled water.

C9_ChemistrySymbolsofelementsSim.title: Chemical symbols can be written using all capital letters
C9_ChemistrySymbolsofelementsSim.description: Students believe that both letters of a two-letter chemical symbol can be written in uppercase without altering its fundamental meaning.
C9_ChemistrySymbolsofelementsSim.correction: According to IUPAC rules, the first letter of a chemical symbol is always uppercase, while the second letter must be lowercase. Writing both letters in uppercase changes the representation from an element to a chemical compound, such as CO for carbon monoxide instead of Co for cobalt.

C9_ChemistrySymbolsofelementsSim.title: Element symbols are always derived from their English names
C9_ChemistrySymbolsofelementsSim.description: Students assume that every element's chemical symbol is simply formed using the first one or two letters of its standard English name.
C9_ChemistrySymbolsofelementsSim.correction: While many symbols follow this pattern, several elements derive their symbols from their Latin, Greek, or German names. For instance, Sodium has the symbol Na from its Latin name Natrium, and Potassium uses K from Kalium.

C9_ChemistrySymbolsofelementsSim.title: An element's chemical symbol indicates its combining capacity directly
C9_ChemistrySymbolsofelementsSim.description: Students often confuse an element's chemical symbol with its valency, assuming the symbol itself directly shows its combining capacity or charge.
C9_ChemistrySymbolsofelementsSim.correction: A chemical symbol is merely a standardized shorthand notation used to represent one atom of an element. Valency is a property determined by the number of valence electrons involved in bond formation and is not explicitly displayed within the element's symbol.

C9_ChemistrySymbolsofelementsSim.title: Symbols of diatomic elements must always include subscript numbers
C9_ChemistrySymbolsofelementsSim.description: Students frequently confuse atomic symbols with molecular formulas, believing the official symbol for elements like oxygen or hydrogen is O2 or H2.
C9_ChemistrySymbolsofelementsSim.correction: An element's chemical symbol represents a single atom, such as O for oxygen or H for hydrogen. Notation like O2 represents a diatomic molecule consisting of two bonded oxygen atoms, which is a molecular formula rather than the atomic symbol.

C9_ChemistrySymbolsofelementsSim.title: Chemical symbols can vary across different countries and languages
C9_ChemistrySymbolsofelementsSim.description: Students think chemical symbols change based on local language translations of element names in different regions of the world.
C9_ChemistrySymbolsofelementsSim.correction: The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) standardizes chemical symbols globally to ensure universal scientific communication. Although an element's full name may vary across different languages, its chemical symbol remains identical in every periodic table worldwide.

C10_ChemistryAlkanesgeneralformulaandpre.title: General formula CnH2n+2 applies to all saturated hydrocarbons
C10_ChemistryAlkanesgeneralformulaandpre.description: Students often believe that the general formula CnH2n+2 applies to all saturated hydrocarbons, including cyclic alkanes like cyclohexane.
C10_ChemistryAlkanesgeneralformulaandpre.correction: The general formula CnH2n+2 specifically applies only to open-chain (acyclic) alkanes. Cyclic alkanes lose two hydrogen atoms to form a ring structure, giving them the general formula CnH2n despite containing only single C-C bonds.

C10_ChemistryAlkanesgeneralformulaandpre.title: Wurtz reaction efficiently prepares methane and odd carbon alkanes
C10_ChemistryAlkanesgeneralformulaandpre.description: Students frequently assume that the Wurtz reaction can be used to prepare any alkane, including methane and unsymmetrical odd-carbon alkanes, with high yield.
C10_ChemistryAlkanesgeneralformulaandpre.correction: Methane cannot be prepared via the Wurtz reaction because the mechanism requires coupling two alkyl groups, yielding a minimum of two carbon atoms. Additionally, using a mixture of two different alkyl halides produces a mixture of three different alkanes that are difficult to separate, making it impractical for preparing odd-carbon alkanes.

C10_ChemistryAlkanesgeneralformulaandpre.title: Decarboxylation yields alkanes with the same carbon count
C10_ChemistryAlkanesgeneralformulaandpre.description: Students often believe that heating a sodium salt of a carboxylic acid with soda lime produces an alkane with the exact same number of carbon atoms.
C10_ChemistryAlkanesgeneralformulaandpre.correction: Decarboxylation involves the removal of the carboxyl group (-COONa) as sodium carbonate (Na2CO3). Consequently, the resulting alkane always contains one less carbon atom than the parent carboxylic acid sodium salt.

C10_ChemistryAlkanesgeneralformulaandpre.title: Hydrogenation breaks carbon carbon single bonds to form methane
C10_ChemistryAlkanesgeneralformulaandpre.description: Students sometimes believe that catalytic hydrogenation breaks carbon-carbon single bonds in higher alkenes or alkynes to reduce them down to methane.
C10_ChemistryAlkanesgeneralformulaandpre.correction: Catalytic hydrogenation only adds hydrogen atoms across carbon-carbon double or triple bonds to saturate the organic molecule. It does not cleave carbon-carbon single bonds, meaning the resulting alkane retains the exact same carbon chain length as the reactant.

C10_ChemistryAlkanesgeneralformulaandpre.title: Combustion of alkanes always yields carbon dioxide and water
C10_ChemistryAlkanesgeneralformulaandpre.description: Students often believe that burning any alkane will always result in complete combustion, producing only carbon dioxide and water vapor regardless of conditions.
C10_ChemistryAlkanesgeneralformulaandpre.correction: Complete combustion producing carbon dioxide and water occurs only when an excess supply of oxygen is available. In a limited supply of oxygen, incomplete combustion occurs, leading to the formation of toxic carbon monoxide gas or unburnt carbon soot alongside water.

C9_ChemistryLaboratorypreparationofhydro.title: Concentrated Nitric Acid Can Prepare Hydrogen Gas in Labs
C9_ChemistryLaboratorypreparationofhydro.description: Students believe that any acid, including concentrated nitric acid, can react with zinc to produce hydrogen gas in the laboratory. They assume all acids react similarly with active metals to liberate hydrogen gas.
C9_ChemistryLaboratorypreparationofhydro.correction: Concentrated nitric acid is a powerful oxidizing agent that rapidly oxidizes hydrogen gas into water as soon as it forms. Consequently, the reaction yields oxides of nitrogen rather than hydrogen gas. Therefore, dilute hydrochloric acid or dilute sulfuric acid must be used for laboratory hydrogen preparation.

C9_ChemistryLaboratorypreparationofhydro.title: Hydrogen Gas Is Collected by Downward Displacement of Air
C9_ChemistryLaboratorypreparationofhydro.description: Students often assume that hydrogen gas is collected by downward displacement of air simply because it is lighter than air.
C9_ChemistryLaboratorypreparationofhydro.correction: Hydrogen forms an explosive mixture when mixed with atmospheric oxygen, making collection by air displacement extremely hazardous. Additionally, hydrogen diffuses rapidly into air, preventing efficient collection. Instead, it is collected by the downward displacement of water because hydrogen is virtually insoluble in water.

C9_ChemistryLaboratorypreparationofhydro.title: Pure Zinc Is Preferred Over Granulated Zinc for Reaction
C9_ChemistryLaboratorypreparationofhydro.description: Students think that chemically pure zinc metal is superior to granulated zinc for preparing hydrogen gas efficiently.
C9_ChemistryLaboratorypreparationofhydro.correction: Pure zinc reacts extremely slowly with dilute acids, resulting in a negligible rate of gas evolution. Granulated zinc contains trace copper impurities that form local electrochemical cells, significantly accelerating the reaction rate. Furthermore, the granulated form provides a larger surface area for faster hydrogen production.

C9_ChemistryLaboratorypreparationofhydro.title: Hydrogen Gas Acts as a Supporter of Combustion
C9_ChemistryLaboratorypreparationofhydro.description: Students often confuse being combustible with supporting combustion, assuming hydrogen helps other substances burn.
C9_ChemistryLaboratorypreparationofhydro.correction: Hydrogen gas is combustible, meaning it burns in oxygen with a characteristic pop sound and pale blue flame. However, it does not support combustion, so a burning splinter inserted inside a gas jar filled with pure hydrogen is immediately extinguished. Only the hydrogen gas itself burns at the mouth of the jar where oxygen is present.

C9_ChemistryLaboratorypreparationofhydro.title: Initial Gas Bubbles Collected Are Pure Hydrogen Gas
C9_ChemistryLaboratorypreparationofhydro.description: Students assume that the gas coming out of the delivery tube immediately upon reaction start is pure hydrogen ready for collection.
C9_ChemistryLaboratorypreparationofhydro.correction: The gas escaping initially consists mainly of air originally present inside the flask, forming a dangerous explosive air-hydrogen mixture. Bringing a flame near the tube during this phase can cause the entire apparatus to explode. The first few bubbles must be allowed to escape until pure hydrogen completely purges the air from the apparatus.

C10_ChemistryClassificationofbasesSim.title: Equating Water Solubility or High Concentration with Base Strength
C10_ChemistryClassificationofbasesSim.description: Students often believe that if a base dissolves completely in water or is highly concentrated, it must automatically be classified as a strong base.
C10_ChemistryClassificationofbasesSim.correction: Base strength depends on the extent of ionization in water, not on solubility or concentration. A strong base dissociates completely into hydroxide ions, whereas a weak base ionizes only partially. For example, a dilute solution of sodium hydroxide remains a strong base, while concentrated ammonium hydroxide is still a weak base.

C10_ChemistryClassificationofbasesSim.title: Believing a Chemical Formula Must Contain Hydroxide to Be a Base
C10_ChemistryClassificationofbasesSim.description: Students frequently assume that compounds lacking an explicit OH group in their chemical formula cannot act as bases.
C10_ChemistryClassificationofbasesSim.correction: According to the Arrhenius theory, bases produce hydroxide ions in water, but broader definitions like Brønsted-Lowry and Lewis classify bases based on proton acceptance and electron-pair donation. Ammonia (NH₃) lacks a hydroxide group in its formula but acts as a base by accepting a proton or donating a lone pair. Therefore, a chemical formula does not need an structural OH group to be classified as a base.

C10_ChemistryClassificationofbasesSim.title: Assuming pH Value Depends Solely on Base Strength Regardless of Concentration
C10_ChemistryClassificationofbasesSim.description: Students commonly think that a strong base will always have a higher pH than a weak base in any given solution.
C10_ChemistryClassificationofbasesSim.correction: The pH of a solution measures the actual concentration of hydrogen or hydroxide ions present, which depends on both the strength and the molar concentration of the base. A highly concentrated solution of a weak base can produce more hydroxide ions and have a higher pH than a very dilute solution of a strong base. Base strength reflects the degree of dissociation, whereas pH reflects total effective ion concentration.

C10_ChemistryClassificationofbasesSim.title: Believing Weak Bases Do Not Ionize or Produce Hydroxide Ions
C10_ChemistryClassificationofbasesSim.description: Students often misunderstand 'weak' to mean that a base does not ionize at all or fails to yield hydroxide ions in aqueous solution.
C10_ChemistryClassificationofbasesSim.correction: Weak bases do ionize in water to yield hydroxide ions, but they do so incompletely, establishing a dynamic equilibrium between molecules and ions. Typically, only a small percentage of molecules dissociate in a weak base solution. As a result, aqueous solutions of weak bases still contain hydroxide ions and can conduct electricity, albeit less effectively than strong bases.

C10_ChemistryClassificationofbasesSim.title: Thinking Lewis Bases Must Only Be Negatively Charged Chemical Species
C10_ChemistryClassificationofbasesSim.description: Students frequently believe that Lewis bases must carry a negative charge because they donate electron pairs to form coordinate bonds.
C10_ChemistryClassificationofbasesSim.correction: A Lewis base is defined as any chemical species that can donate a pair of non-bonding electrons to an electron acceptor. While negative anions like chloride or hydroxide are Lewis bases, neutral molecules with lone pairs such as water and ammonia are also classic Lewis bases. Charge is not a requirement as long as unshared valence electrons are available for donation.

C10_ChemistryElectrolysisofspecificcompo.title: Pure Water Undergoes Electrolysis Easily Without Adding Any Electrolyte
C10_ChemistryElectrolysisofspecificcompo.description: Students believe that pure distilled water is a good conductor of electricity and can readily be electrolyzed on its own.
C10_ChemistryElectrolysisofspecificcompo.correction: Pure water is a extremely weak electrolyte that ionizes negligibly into hydrogen and hydroxyl ions, making it a poor conductor of electricity. A small amount of dilute sulfuric acid or an ionic salt must be added to provide sufficient free ions for conductivity. Acidified water then electrolyzes to release hydrogen gas at the cathode and oxygen gas at the anode.

C10_ChemistryElectrolysisofspecificcompo.title: Electrolysis of Brine Solution Produces Sodium Metal at Cathode
C10_ChemistryElectrolysisofspecificcompo.description: Students assume that electrolyzing aqueous sodium chloride yields sodium metal at the cathode, just like the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride.
C10_ChemistryElectrolysisofspecificcompo.correction: In aqueous sodium chloride, both sodium ions and hydrogen ions from water compete for reduction at the cathode. Because hydrogen ions have a lower discharge potential than sodium ions, hydrogen gas is preferentially liberated at the cathode. Sodium metal can only be obtained through the electrolysis of dry molten sodium chloride.

C10_ChemistryElectrolysisofspecificcompo.title: Blue Color of CuSO4 Solution Stays Constant With Inert Electrodes
C10_ChemistryElectrolysisofspecificcompo.description: Students think the blue color of aqueous copper sulphate solution remains unchanged during electrolysis regardless of whether platinum or copper electrodes are used.
C10_ChemistryElectrolysisofspecificcompo.correction: When inert platinum or carbon electrodes are used, copper ions are discharged at the cathode while hydroxyl ions/water are oxidized at the anode, causing the blue color to fade as copper ion concentration decreases. The blue color remains unchanged only when active copper electrodes are used, because copper dissolves from the anode at the exact same rate it deposits on the cathode.

C10_ChemistryElectrolysisofspecificcompo.title: Positively Charged Cations Always Migrate to the Positive Anode
C10_ChemistryElectrolysisofspecificcompo.description: Students often confuse electrode polarity and assume cations move to the anode because both terms start with similar root words.
C10_ChemistryElectrolysisofspecificcompo.correction: In an electrolytic cell, the cathode is connected to the negative terminal of the DC battery and the anode is connected to the positive terminal. Opposites attract, so positively charged cations migrate toward the negative cathode, while negatively charged anions migrate toward the positive anode.

C10_ChemistryElectrolysisofspecificcompo.title: Mass Deposited at Electrodes Depends Primarily on Applied Voltage
C10_ChemistryElectrolysisofspecificcompo.description: Students assume that increasing the potential difference (voltage) of the power source directly determines how much substance is deposited at an electrode.
C10_ChemistryElectrolysisofspecificcompo.correction: According to Faraday's First Law of Electrolysis, the mass of a substance liberated at an electrode is directly proportional to the total electric charge passed through the solution. Charge depends on the product of current strength and time passed, not voltage alone. Voltage simply drives the current through the circuit against resistance.

C10_ChemistryAlloysandamalgamsSim.title: Amalgams Are Always Liquid Mixtures Containing Mercury
C10_ChemistryAlloysandamalgamsSim.description: Students often believe that because mercury is a liquid metal at room temperature, any amalgam formed with mercury must also remain liquid.
C10_ChemistryAlloysandamalgamsSim.correction: An amalgam is simply an alloy formed by combining mercury with one or more other metals. Depending on the proportion and constituent elements, many amalgams (such as dental silver amalgam or sodium amalgam) are solid or paste-like at room temperature.

C10_ChemistryAlloysandamalgamsSim.title: Brass and Bronze Have the Exact Same Metal Composition
C10_ChemistryAlloysandamalgamsSim.description: Students frequently confuse brass and bronze, believing both alloys are made interchangeably from copper mixed with either zinc or tin.
C10_ChemistryAlloysandamalgamsSim.correction: Brass is specifically an alloy of copper and zinc, whereas bronze is primarily an alloy of copper and tin. Although both are copper-based, zinc gives brass superior malleability and acoustic properties, while tin gives bronze high resistance to corrosion and wear.

C10_ChemistryAlloysandamalgamsSim.title: Alloys Always Have Higher Melting Points Than Constituent Metals
C10_ChemistryAlloysandamalgamsSim.description: Students tend to believe that creating an alloy always increases all physical properties, including raising the melting point above that of pure metals.
C10_ChemistryAlloysandamalgamsSim.correction: Alloying disrupts the orderly arrangement of atoms in a pure metal, which usually reduces the attractive forces and lowers the overall melting point. A classic example is solder (an alloy of lead and tin), which has a significantly lower melting point than either pure lead or pure tin, making it ideal for joining electrical wires.

C10_ChemistryAlloysandamalgamsSim.title: Alloys Are Chemical Compounds Formed by Fixed Chemical Bonds
C10_ChemistryAlloysandamalgamsSim.description: Students often assume that alloys are chemical compounds with fixed chemical formulas formed through chemical reactions between constituent elements.
C10_ChemistryAlloysandamalgamsSim.correction: Alloys are homogeneous solid solutions or physical mixtures, not chemical compounds, meaning their elemental proportions can vary continuously. Because no new chemical bonds are created, alloys retain the basic chemical characteristics of their constituent elements while modifying physical properties like electrical conductivity, hardness, and ductility.

C10_ChemistryAlloysandamalgamsSim.title: Interstitial Alloys Form by Replacing Host Metal Atoms Directly
C10_ChemistryAlloysandamalgamsSim.description: Students frequently confuse interstitial and substitutional alloys, believing interstitial alloys involve swapping host metal lattice atoms with smaller solute atoms.
C10_ChemistryAlloysandamalgamsSim.correction: In substitutional alloys (like brass), solute atoms of similar atomic radius replace host metal atoms directly in the crystal lattice. In interstitial alloys, significantly smaller atoms (such as carbon in steel) fit into the tiny void spaces or 'interstices' between host metal atoms without replacing them.

C10_ChemistryPeriodicpropertiesatomicsiz.title: Atomic size increases across a period with increasing atomic number
C10_ChemistryPeriodicpropertiesatomicsiz.description: Students often believe that adding more protons and electrons across a period makes the atom heavier and physically larger. They assume that a higher atomic number automatically leads to a larger atomic radius.
C10_ChemistryPeriodicpropertiesatomicsiz.correction: Across a period, valence electrons are added to the same shell while the number of protons in the nucleus increases. This higher nuclear charge increases the effective nuclear charge ($Z_{eff}$), pulling the valence shell closer to the nucleus and causing atomic size to decrease from left to right.

C10_ChemistryPeriodicpropertiesatomicsiz.title: Cations are larger than their neutral parent atoms
C10_ChemistryPeriodicpropertiesatomicsiz.description: Students frequently think that forming a cation increases atomic size because of changes in electron repulsion or positive charge expansion. Some assume the size remains unchanged because the element's identity stays the same.
C10_ChemistryPeriodicpropertiesatomicsiz.correction: A cation is always smaller than its neutral parent atom. The loss of valence electrons often results in the complete removal of the outermost shell. Furthermore, the remaining electrons experience a greater effective nuclear charge per electron, pulling them tighter toward the nucleus.

C10_ChemistryPeriodicpropertiesatomicsiz.title: Effective nuclear charge is identical to total nuclear charge
C10_ChemistryPeriodicpropertiesatomicsiz.description: Students often assume valence electrons experience the full attractive pull of all protons present in the nucleus. They ignore the shielding effect caused by inner-shell electrons.
C10_ChemistryPeriodicpropertiesatomicsiz.correction: Inner shell electrons shield outer valence electrons from the full positive charge of the nucleus. The effective nuclear charge ($Z_{eff}$) is the net positive charge experienced by an electron, which is equal to the total nuclear charge minus the shielding constant ($Z_{eff} = Z - S$). Therefore, valence electrons feel a smaller pull than the total nuclear charge.

C10_ChemistryPeriodicpropertiesatomicsiz.title: Isoelectronic ions have identical radii due to equal electrons
C10_ChemistryPeriodicpropertiesatomicsiz.description: Students believe that since isoelectronic species possess the same number of electrons and identical electronic configurations, their ionic sizes must be equal. They overlook the effect of differing numbers of protons in their nuclei.
C10_ChemistryPeriodicpropertiesatomicsiz.correction: Although isoelectronic ions have the same number of electrons, their nuclear charges differ based on their atomic numbers. An ion with more protons exerts a stronger attractive force on the same set of electrons, drawing them closer. Consequently, species with higher atomic numbers in an isoelectronic series have smaller ionic radii.

C10_ChemistryPeriodicpropertiesatomicsiz.title: Atomic size decreases down a group from increasing nuclear charge
C10_ChemistryPeriodicpropertiesatomicsiz.description: Students sometimes reason that because atomic number increases substantially down a group, the larger positive nuclear charge pulls electrons closer, shrinking the atom. They prioritize nuclear charge over energy levels.
C10_ChemistryPeriodicpropertiesatomicsiz.correction: Moving down a group, a completely new principal energy level (shell) is added at each successive element. The increase in distance caused by adding electron shells far outweighs the pull from the increasing nuclear charge. As a result, the atomic radius consistently increases down a group.

C11_ChemistryAlkenespreparationandstruct.title: Pi Bonds Formed by Overlap of sp2 Hybrid Orbitals
C11_ChemistryAlkenespreparationandstruct.description: Students often believe that both the sigma and pi bonds in an alkene double bond are formed by the overlap of sp2 hybridized orbitals.
C11_ChemistryAlkenespreparationandstruct.correction: In sp2 hybridized carbon atoms, only three sp2 hybrid orbitals are formed to make sigma bonds in a planar geometry. The pi bond is formed by the lateral (sideways) overlap of unhybridized p-orbitals that remain perpendicular to the plane of the sp2 hybrid orbitals. Therefore, hybrid orbitals never form pi bonds.

C11_ChemistryAlkenespreparationandstruct.title: Alcohol Dehydration Always Yields a Single Unique Alkene Product
C11_ChemistryAlkenespreparationandstruct.description: Students frequently think that acid-catalyzed dehydration of an unsymmetrical alcohol yields only one alkene product without any structural rearrangements.
C11_ChemistryAlkenespreparationandstruct.correction: Dehydration of alcohols proceeds via a carbocation intermediate, which can undergo 1,2-hydride or 1,2-methyl shifts to form a more stable carbocation. Additionally, elimination can occur from different beta-carbons, leading to a mixture of isomeric alkenes. The major product is predicted by Saytzeff's rule, favoring the more substituted, stable alkene.

C11_ChemistryAlkenespreparationandstruct.title: Dehydrohalogenation Removes Hydrogen from Carbon with More Hydrogens
C11_ChemistryAlkenespreparationandstruct.description: Students often misapply elimination rules and assume that dehydrohalogenation removes a beta-hydrogen from the carbon atom that already has more hydrogen atoms.
C11_ChemistryAlkenespreparationandstruct.correction: According to Saytzeff's (Zaitsev's) rule, dehydrohalogenation primarily eliminates hydrogen from the beta-carbon that has fewer hydrogen atoms. This selective elimination yields the highly substituted and thermodynamically more stable alkene as the major product. Hofmann product formation (removal from the carbon with more hydrogens) is an exception that occurs mainly with bulky bases.

C11_ChemistryAlkenespreparationandstruct.title: Free Rotation Exists Around Carbon Carbon Double Bonds
C11_ChemistryAlkenespreparationandstruct.description: Students often assume that groups attached to a carbon-carbon double bond can freely rotate just like they do around single bonds in alkanes.
C11_ChemistryAlkenespreparationandstruct.correction: The formation of a pi bond requires continuous parallel sideways overlap of unhybridized p-orbitals above and below the molecular plane. Rotating one carbon relative to the other would break this pi overlap, which requires a significant amount of energy. Consequently, rotation is restricted, locking the sp2 carbon framework in a rigid plane and giving rise to geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism.

C11_ChemistryAlkenespreparationandstruct.title: Pi Bonds Are Stronger Than Sigma Bonds in Alkenes
C11_ChemistryAlkenespreparationandstruct.description: Students often assume that because a C=C double bond is stronger overall than a C-C single bond, the constituent pi bond must be stronger than the sigma bond.
C11_ChemistryAlkenespreparationandstruct.correction: Although a double bond is stronger than a single bond as a whole, an individual pi bond is significantly weaker than a sigma bond. Sigma bonds result from direct coaxial (head-on) overlap of orbitals, whereas pi bonds result from parallel collateral (sideways) overlap, which is inherently less effective. This relative weakness of the pi bond is why alkenes are much more chemically reactive than alkanes.

C10_ChemistryPolarandnonpolarcovalentcom.title: Presence of Polar Bonds Guarantees a Polar Molecule
C10_ChemistryPolarandnonpolarcovalentcom.description: Students believe that if a molecule contains polar covalent bonds, the molecule as a whole must be polar. They fail to consider how molecular geometry affects overall polarity.
C10_ChemistryPolarandnonpolarcovalentcom.correction: A molecule can contain polar covalent bonds and still be non-polar overall if its molecular geometry is symmetrical. In symmetrical molecules like carbon dioxide (CO₂) or carbon tetrachloride (CCl₄), individual bond dipoles pull equally in opposite directions and cancel each other out. This results in a net dipole moment of zero, making the overall molecule non-polar.

C10_ChemistryPolarandnonpolarcovalentcom.title: Non-Polar Covalent Bonds Only Form Between Identical Atoms
C10_ChemistryPolarandnonpolarcovalentcom.description: Students often assume that non-polar covalent bonds can only exist between two identical non-metal atoms, such as in O₂ or N₂. They incorrectly believe that any bond between different elements must be polar.
C10_ChemistryPolarandnonpolarcovalentcom.correction: Non-polar covalent bonds can also form between different elements if their electronegativity values are nearly equal. For instance, the carbon-hydrogen (C-H) bond in methane (CH₄) is non-polar because carbon and hydrogen have very similar electronegativities. Therefore, equal sharing of electrons can occur between distinct non-metal atoms.

C10_ChemistryPolarandnonpolarcovalentcom.title: Dipole Moment Is Calculated by Simple Scalar Addition
C10_ChemistryPolarandnonpolarcovalentcom.description: Students view molecular dipole moment as a scalar sum of bond polarities rather than a vector quantity. Consequently, they assume molecules with more polar bonds always possess higher net dipole moments.
C10_ChemistryPolarandnonpolarcovalentcom.correction: Dipole moment is a vector quantity that has both magnitude and direction. The net dipole moment of a molecule is the vector sum of all individual bond dipoles in three-dimensional space. Because vectors can reinforce or negate each other based on bond angles, spatial geometry dictates the final dipole moment.

C10_ChemistryPolarandnonpolarcovalentcom.title: Covalent Compounds Never Dissolve in Water Environment
C10_ChemistryPolarandnonpolarcovalentcom.description: Students frequently assume that all covalent compounds are insoluble in water because water only dissolves ionic solids. They fail to distinguish between polar and non-polar covalent solute behavior.
C10_ChemistryPolarandnonpolarcovalentcom.correction: Solubility follows the principle of 'like dissolves like,' meaning polar solvents dissolve polar solutes. While non-polar covalent compounds are insoluble in water, polar covalent compounds like glucose, ethanol, and hydrogen chloride dissolve readily. These polar solutes form strong dipole-dipole interactions or hydrogen bonds with polar water molecules.

C10_ChemistryPolarandnonpolarcovalentcom.title: Polar Covalent Liquids Conduct Electricity in Pure State
C10_ChemistryPolarandnonpolarcovalentcom.description: Students believe that pure polar covalent liquids conduct electricity easily because they contain partial positive and negative charges. They confuse partial charges on bound atoms with free-moving ions.
C10_ChemistryPolarandnonpolarcovalentcom.correction: Conduction of electricity requires mobile charged particles, such as free ions or free electrons. Partial charges in polar covalent molecules are fixed within the chemical bonds and cannot carry an electric current in the pure liquid state. Polar covalent compounds like pure liquid HCl only conduct electricity when dissolved in water, where they ionize to form mobile hydronium and chloride ions.

C10_ChemistrySulphuricacidContactprocess.title: Direct Dissolution of Sulfur Trioxide in Water Forms Sulfuric Acid
C10_ChemistrySulphuricacidContactprocess.description: Students often believe that sulfur trioxide gas is directly dissolved in water to yield sulfuric acid in the Contact Process. They assume this direct hydration is used industrially because it matches the simple balanced chemical equation.
C10_ChemistrySulphuricacidContactprocess.correction: Direct reaction of sulfur trioxide with water is violently exothermic and creates a dense mist of fine acid droplets that is extremely difficult to condense. To prevent this safety hazard and loss of product, sulfur trioxide is absorbed in 98% concentrated sulfuric acid to produce oleum (H2S2O7). Oleum is then safely diluted with calculated amounts of water to yield sulfuric acid of the desired concentration.

C10_ChemistrySulphuricacidContactprocess.title: Vanadium Pentoxide Catalyst Increases Final Yield of Sulfur Trioxide
C10_ChemistrySulphuricacidContactprocess.description: Students frequently assume that adding Vanadium Pentoxide (V2O5) increases the final percentage yield of sulfur trioxide. They confuse the rate of a chemical reaction with its equilibrium position.
C10_ChemistrySulphuricacidContactprocess.correction: A catalyst speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally, reducing the time taken to reach equilibrium without altering the equilibrium yield. The high yield of sulfur trioxide is controlled by Le Chatelier's principle through optimized temperature, pressure, and reactant concentrations. V2O5 simply allows the system to reach equilibrium rapidly at an economically viable operating temperature.

C10_ChemistrySulphuricacidContactprocess.title: Higher Temperatures Yield More Sulfur Trioxide in Contact Process
C10_ChemistrySulphuricacidContactprocess.description: Students often think that heating the reaction chamber to extremely high temperatures yields more sulfur trioxide gas rapidly. They believe higher kinetic energy always favors higher product formation in industrial setups.
